prompt:
Find real, published studies on whether people with ADHD benefit from using AI assistants for task initiation or executive function. Cite the studies and quote their findings.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
I searched for published, peer-reviewed studies specifically examining whether people with ADHD benefit from AI assistants for task initiation or executive function. Below are the results, including several "near-misses" that are often cited in this space but do not actually measure AI assistant usage.

SOURCE: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10870547211046197 | QUOTE: "Preliminary evidence suggests that digital mental health interventions may be feasible and acceptable for adults with ADHD." | CLAIM: Digital interventions broadly (not specifically AI assistants) show preliminary feasibility/acceptability for adults with ADHD.

SOURCE: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/brb3.2410 | QUOTE: "AI-based interventions show promising results in improving the cognitive and social skills of children with neurodevelopmental disorders." | CLAIM: AI-based interventions show promise for cognitive/social skills in children with neurodevelopmental disorders broadly (including but not limited to ADHD); does not specify task initiation or executive function outcomes.

SOURCE: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10870547231153328 | QUOTE: "This study did not examine the efficacy or effectiveness of these apps for ADHD management." | CLAIM: This content analysis of ADHD apps explicitly excluded efficacy testing; cannot be used as evidence that apps/AI assistants improve task initiation or executive function.

SOURCE: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00702-022-02525-0 | QUOTE: "The objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of a computerized cognitive training program (Cogmed) in improving executive functions in children with ADHD." | CLAIM: Studies computerized cognitive training (game-based working memory tasks), not AI assistants; examines executive function broadly but not task initiation via AI assistants.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: Any randomized controlled trial or quasi-experimental study measuring the effect of AI assistants (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, virtual assistants) on task initiation specifically in adults or children diagnosed with ADHD.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: Any peer-reviewed study examining real-world usage patterns of AI assistants for executive function scaffolding in ADHD populations with pre-post behavioral outcome measures.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: Any systematic review or meta-analysis specifically isolating "AI assistants" (as distinct from generic mobile apps or computerized cognitive training) as an intervention for ADHD-related executive dysfunction.

**Key Finding:** There appears to be a significant gap in the empirical literature. While there is substantial research on (a) digital mental health interventions for ADHD generally, (b) AI applications for autism and other neurodevelopmental conditions, and (c) computerized cognitive training for ADHD, I could not locate any published study that specifically investigates whether people with ADHD use or benefit from AI assistants (such as large language model-based chatbots or virtual assistants) for task initiation or executive function support. The existing literature consists primarily of app content analyses (which measure features, not outcomes) and studies of structured cognitive training programs (which are distinct from generative AI assistants).
